title: Being a Beginner Is Awesome
author: Stoic Wisdoms
summary: This essay argues that adults gradually lose the willingness to be bad at things, because competence becomes part of identity and being a beginner starts to feel like a verdict on ourselves. The author traces how a childhood spent constantly learning gives way to a narrowing circle of things we already do well, with phrases like I'm just not that kind of person hardening into supposed fact. He then makes the case for beginnerhood: progress is fast and visible, which rebuilds confidence in our capacity to learn, and effortful struggle can be more productive than it feels, citing Robert Bjork's desirable difficulties. A beginner also has no reputation to protect and sees the world with fresh attention, but the window is brief. He closes with Epictetus's advice that anyone who wants to make progress must be content to be thought foolish, and invites the reader to try something new. Archived under Leadership as personal growth and self-improvement writing.
points: Adult reluctance to start something new is identity protection: competence becomes self-image, so being bad at something feels personal and I'm not that kind of person hardens into fact.
Early progress is fast and visible, and watching effort turn into ability week by week rebuilds trust in your own capacity to learn.
Drawing on Bjork's desirable difficulties, the author notes that performance in a lesson is a poor guide to learning, since struggle can pay off a week later.
Beginners enjoy freedom from reputation and the renewed attention of newcomers, but both fade quickly as skill becomes automatic.
Epictetus's advice to be content to be thought foolish generalizes: the wish to appear competent eventually caps what we are willing to attempt.
quotes: I hope you never reach a point in life where you stop being willing to start from scratch. I know how good it feels to be capable, to know what you’re doing and feel confident in your abilities.

Something changes when we get older. We become good at a handful of things, usually our work and whatever we spent our younger years doing. Over time, those abilities become part of how we see ourselves.
We rarely describe it that way. We say we have no ear for languages or that we’re too old to start.
At the beginning, progress is rarely hard to see. In the first few weeks of swimming, you might go from struggling to coordinate your breathing to reaching the other end of the pool without stopping.
The psychologist Robert Bjork studied how certain kinds of effortful practice can improve long-term learning, even when performance feels worse in the moment. He called these “desirable difficulties.
There’s also a freedom in having no reputation to protect. Nobody expects a beginner to know what they’re doing.

If we only pursue things we’re already good at, our lives gradually narrow around the abilities we happen to have. We may become extremely capable within that small territory, while entire experiences remain unknown to us because we were unwilling to feel incompetent for a little while.
Epictetus told his students that if they wanted to make progress, they had to be content to be thought foolish. He was speaking about philosophy, but I think his advice reaches much further.
